E1903.summary: Man's life-spirit, impure by birth, which the alchemical work purifies, dissolves, ferments and circulates until it is promoted to perfection and ends in the Principle of things.
E1903.body:
For Atwood the Vital Spirit is the subject the work acts on. It is promoted by the art “from one form of being into another” through many stages to perfection [I.2 ¶48]. It must be segregated from the defilements and sense-impressions implanted by birth: the aim is “to segregate the Vital Spirit away from those defilements and imaginative impressures” [II.2 ¶8], and the ancients began by “purifying the Vital Spirit in its proper Light” [II.2 ¶24].

After the first preliminaries “the object was to produce an alteration in the Vital Spirit” by Rational Analysis [III.1 ¶50]; yet “Nothing is done radically to meliorate the Vital Spirit” without a motive, which comes from its being deprived of its Understanding Light [III.1 ¶28]. It undergoes a “spontaneous fermentation” that changes the Passive Subject, and by grafting and transplanting could be grown and sublimed by degrees [III.1 ¶9]. Its dissolution and the alienation of its natural bind discover the True matter [III.2 ¶62]. Purified “through sacrifice of all foreign attractions”, it revolves about its center with active and passive power united [III.3 ¶3]; it may lawfully “descend and ascend in successive circulations” until it ends in the Principle of things [II.4 ¶52]. Atwood says that, it would seem, the whole secret “consists in the sanquinary circulation of the Vital Spirit” under a threefold Law [III.3 ¶72]. In the colour process one works with it, and “This Spirit is so full of life” that adding more renews a failed stage [II.1 ¶25].

Sendivogius places the soul “in the vital spirit in the purest blood” [II.1 ¶10]; an unattributed passage calls it “the vital spirit of the arterial blood”, where the three principles are unequally composed and opposition ceases in the blackening [II.1 ¶21].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says it is “in the Universal as well as in the individual” [APP ¶28], that “the human vital spirit” is what Alchemy ferments and purifies [APP ¶68], and that it “always is in chaos, i.e., always coming to be, never is, and whilst in this life wants the rebirth” [APP ¶165].

E1904.summary: The transmutation of life; Atwood says the Aristaeus myth bears on it in an advanced stage.
E1904.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood says the Aristaeus myth “bears altogether on the Vital transmutation in an advanced stage” [APP ¶173].

E1905.summary: Vital power, which Atwood says is capable of illimitable artificial increase.
E1905.body: Atwood speaks of “the illimitable powers and artificial increase of vitalization”, conceivable to those who apply a fragment of the same virtue benevolently [IV.3 ¶35].

E1906.summary: In Khunrath, named with the Green Duenech as the true matters of the Blessed Stone.
E1906.body: Khunrath (quoted) names “the Green Duenech and the Vitriol of Venus, which are the true matters of the Blessed Stone” [IV.1 ¶36].

E1907.summary: The life-giving essence of the Stone, of the same origin as what it assimilates, the Universal Spirit; called azoth by the Hermetic philosophers.
E1907.body: Atwood: “this powerful vivific Ens is of the same origin as that which it assimilates --- viz., the Universal Spirit”, and it draws the Homogeneal Nature into itself [IV.3 ¶29]. Identified with azoth: “the Hermetic philosophers have given it the name of azoth, which adheres to bodies” [IV.3 ¶29].

forms: the Voice at our Lord's baptism
E1908.summary: The Voice at our Lord's baptism and our Lord's prayer, which Atwood cites in the Table Talk to illustrate the Name speaking and working its change.
E1908.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood cites the Voice and Christ's prayer (“Father, glorify thy Name”; “Now is my soul troubled”) to illustrate the Name speaking and working its change, and Christ needing new strength by its utterance: “How I have both glorified my Name and I will glorify it again” [APP ¶88].

E1909.summary: The only way, Atwood reports it taught, to become partaker of the Divinity one aspires to; also the means by which the torch promotes things to their utmost strength.
E1909.body: Atwood reports the teaching that “no otherwise can we be made partakers, it is taught, but by a voluntary assimilation” [III.4 ¶20]. Of the torch's action she writes: “by its voluntary assimilation, increasing and promoting things to their utmost boundary of strength” [IV.4 ¶32].

E1910.summary: That through which Osiris, the Divine Light, passes in the regeneration, suffering Typhon's restraint and subversion.
E1910.body: Atwood says Osiris (the Divine Light) “suffers in passing through the voluntary axle in the regeneration”, undergoing Typhon's restraint, contrariety and subversion [III.1 ¶63]. The expression is not further explained.

E1911.summary: That in which, Atwood says, the central hidden light is hidden.
E1911.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “the central hidden light (there’s the mystery) is hidden in the voluntary contrariation” [APP ¶125]. The sentence is broken; it appears to link this to Saturn or the Will.

E1912.summary: The agent applied to obliterate the defilements of the Universal Element, first in a series with gentleness, beneficence and justice.
E1912.body: Atwood: “By applying the proper voluntary corrosive they teach to obliterate its defilements”, i.e. those of the Universal Element; it stands first in a series followed by gentleness, beneficence and justice [IV.1 ¶47].

E1913.summary: Something drawn upward into intellectual reminiscence once the vital medium is dissolved; Wisdom's lost Efficient recovered in the Light of life.
E1913.body: Atwood says the dissolution of the vital medium “draws the Voluntary Efficient upward into intellectual reminescence” [III.1 ¶23], and speaks of “Wisdom recovering her lost Efficient in the Light of life” [III.1 ¶36]. The term is not further defined.

E1914.summary: In Atwood's reading, Motion: the lame god who stirs up the fire, instrument of the mind; also the fire of the work, which destroys and maintains life.
E1914.body:
Atwood identifies Vulcan with Motion, “which the lame god personates” [IV.1 ¶34]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) she states: “The Vulcan of the Alchemists is Motion.” He is lame because motion in this life is halting and never returns into its own principle, and “Vulcan is not the fire, the ignis Philosophorum, but the stirrer up of the fire.” [APP ¶129]. Further: “The Vulcan or Faber is the instrument of the motive agent --- the mind.” [APP ¶130].

In the monk's words, “Fire only can effect that, and Vulcan is the sole and only master of all these”: sole separator of good from evil and pure from impure; a Vulcan acts in the Greater Orb and a certain other Vulcan in the Lesser World [IV.1 ¶40]. Vulcan also stands for the fire of the work: “Which Vulcanic action, to destroy life and to maintain it”, and “placing it again upon the coals, stir Vulcan into it” [IV.1 ¶43].

E1915.summary: The alchemists' Matter as first known: full of heterogeneous qualities, fallen from its sphere and defiled, needing preparations, solutions and calcinations.
E1915.body: Reported as the alchemists' view: the Matter as first found is “full of heterogeneous qualities and notions, as a subject fallen from its sphere and defiled”, and so needs preparations, solutions and calcinations [II.2 ¶16].

E1916.summary: Per the Scholiast, the newborn quintessential spirit or Proteus: the first sublimed quintessence not yet perfected by art, the same as the crow in a different estate.
E1916.body: Atwood reports the Scholiast: “The vulture, according to our Scholiast, is the new born quintessential spirit or Proteus” [I.3 n11]. It is the Spirit of life in its active, devouring state: “The vulture is the first sublimed quintessence not yet perfected by art” [I.3 n12]. Identified with the crow: “The vulture and the crow are interpreted to be one and the same thing, only differing somewhat in estate” [I.3 n12].

E1917.summary: An orrery cited as the model of the orrery explanation of the lights of the Mysteries, which Atwood rejects.
E1917.body: Atwood invokes Walker’s or Lloyd’s Eidouranion to contrast with, and reject, the explanation of the lights shown in the Mysteries as an orrery-like display [II.3 ¶49].

E1918.summary: Author of the Divine Legation, whom Atwood criticizes for treating the Mysteries as political fraud but uses on the golden bough and as translator of Stoboeus.
E1918.body: Atwood criticizes Warburton for seeing the Mysteries as political fraud and calls his notions obsolete; the Divine Legation, vol. 1, is also cited as a reference [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n1, II.2 n8]. His account of the institution she calls absurd, citing his phrase “a mere illuminated image, which the priest had purified” [II.4 ¶29]. Yet she draws on him where he supports her: the golden bough was literally part of the sacred equipage, and Aeneid VI alludes to the Mysteries [II.3 ¶11, II.3 ¶13, II.3 n10]. She also uses his translation of the Stoboeus passage, which she calls well rendered (Divine Legation 1:342) [II.3 ¶37, II.3 n42].

E1919.summary: Intricate structures constructed by and for the Key, for it alone to pass through.
E1919.body: Atwood: “those mirific wards which were constructed by it, and for it to pass through, and for it alone” [IV.4 ¶32].

E1920.summary: The philosophers' Water: not common water but the ethereal body of life and light, altered and corporified by art; the middle nature, mercurial quintessence and first matter, under many names.
E1920.body:
**Atwood's account.** The philosophers' water is not common water but “a certain tortured water, having suffered alteration by art and becomes corporified”; “it is the ethereal body of life and light which they profess to have discovered”, heavenly and not wetting the hands [I.2 ¶43]. Into it gold and metals are reduced in the analysis: “all metals, likewise, may be reduced into water, that is, into their first pure matter” [III.2 n38], and “the water, being incorruptible, will require no analogous process” [III.2 ¶48]. The Water of the Adepts is “the miraculous product of the spiritual poles of mind in sublime conjunction at their source”, a regenerate body made manifest by the physico-chemical art: “this was their Stilla roris, Lac Virginis, Elixir, Aqua Vitae, Azoth, Prima Materia Lapis et Rebis” [III.3 ¶73]; “in this water, when destruction has done its worst with the elements of life, the principle of all is artificially preserved” [III.3 ¶71]. Verse quoted with it equates it with Democrit's “Lux umbra caresn, Water most orient” and Hermes' “water of crude Mercury” [III.3 ¶74]. The meadows “bear water which is the symbol of vivification”, one of the “material rewards of initiation” she defers [II.4 ¶16].

**Hermes.** “The water spoken of by Hermes is the passive spirit” [I.3 n21]; “the water was first in the air, then in the earth” [I.3 ¶19]; yet in the Stone “this, however, is not water in its true form, but fire” [I.3 ¶26]. It is “the middle nature, which is the Water” joining Heaven and Earth [I.3 ¶55]; “The water alluded to is the mercurial quintessence”, born “in a humid and vaprous consistency” and golden when informed by the central light [I.3 n63].

**Eirenaeus.** The fire is freed “by the mediation of our water”, and “the first water will work on the body till it hath opened the pores and extracted partly the tincture of Sol” [III.1 ¶14]; the text does not say whether these two waters are the same.

**Synesius.** “that Water is the most sharp vinegar, which makes gold to be a pure spirit”, “that Blessed Nature which engenders all things” [III.1 ¶70]; the sole object of labour, “that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals”, to be decocted gently [III.3 ¶60].

**Boehme.** Desiring fire takes the Light's virtue and “maketh it an essence, viz., Water” [III.3 ¶24].

**Eudoxus.** “Our Water is a living Spring which comes out of the Stone by a natural miracle of our philosophy.” [IV.3 ¶8]. It is “the soul and the spirit” [IV.3 ¶7], called wine, water of life, vinegar or oil “according to the different degrees of Preparation”, “properly called the Vinegar of the Wise”, the “Divine Liquor”, and “the reducer of the soul to its body” [IV.3 ¶8]. Boiling turns it into Earth, the Mercury of the Wise carrying its own Sulphur: “it is this which reduces our Water into Earth”, and as earth it “shall obtain all the virtues which the philosophers attribute to it” [IV.3 ¶12].

E1921.summary: In the Adept's teaching, the two principles present in all things that regenerate and perform the whole work.
E1921.body: The Adept (quoted) says of Water and Spirit: “These two are in all things” and “The two former principles perform all.” The Spirit uses the water to purge and wash its body [IV.2 ¶18].

E1922.summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, the water with which sublimed arsenic and calcined mercury are ground, carrying life and light into them.
E1922.body: Pierce, the Black Monk (quoted): sublimed arsenic and calcined mercury are ground with “the Water of Myght, Which beareth ingression of Lyfe and Light” [III.3 ¶16].

E1923.summary: Sendivogius's name for a water that does not wet the hands, white as snow, which he calls the Water of Life.
E1923.body: Sendivogius (quoted) speaks of those who “call the Water of our Sea, the Water of Life, not wetting the hands”, and says “that water was as white as snow” [III.2 ¶7].

E1924.summary: In Pierce the Black Monk's verse, that which makes the marriage; not explained.
E1924.body: Pierce, the Black Monk (quoted): “But the Water of the Wood, maketh the marriage.” [III.4 ¶21]. Not explained further.

E1925.summary: The fixed watery form of the philosophic matter, a mature state that frames the royal elements; in the Master's words, the blessed form that dissolves the Elements.
E1925.body: Atwood: “The fixed watery Form of the philosophic matter” is a more mature state of one praised earlier, creatrix of the royal elements, drawing to itself the rubified light of its internal agent; “this is the fountain which Berhard Trevisan mentions” [I.3 n39]. The Master (quoted): “O blessed watery Form! That dissolveth the Elements!”; with it a sulphurous Form is taken up and mixed with Acetum, “with this watery soul” [IV.2 ¶14].

E1927.summary: The true philosophic proportions of the work; Hermes says they are the two third waters of the divided Water.
E1927.body: Hermes (quoted): “the two third waters are the Weights of the Wise” [I.3 ¶6]. The Scholiast's note glosses them as “the true philosophic proportions called also by Hermes the Weights of the Wise” [I.3 n6].

E1928.summary: That upon which deviating profane persons may be broken; not explained.
E1928.body: Atwood says deviating profane persons may “become broken necessitiously upon the Wheel of Life” [III.4 ¶9]. Not explained further.

E1929.summary: The two forms of the Stone, fermented respectively with pure silver and with fine gold.
E1929.body: Unattributed: the Stone is fermented “with pure silver for the White, and with Red for fine Gold” [IV.3 ¶29]. Not further explained here.

E1930.summary: In an adept's words, the resting point enjoyed when the colours appear and the king has triumphed over death.
E1930.body: An adept (quoted): “Here thou mayest rest and wait, and enjoy the glory of thy white elixir”, once the colours appear and the king has triumphed over death [I.3 n22].

E1931.summary: The light revealed beneath the influx of the Holy Spirit when the Divine presence arises; Van Helmont's Quellem, the primeval Light.
E1931.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) Atwood says it is revealed beneath the influx of the Holy Spirit when the Divine presence arises: “that wonderful White Light which Van Helmont speaks of, though in a very superficial way, as the Quellem”, belonging “to the Ancient of Days, i.e., the primeval Light.” [APP ¶157].

E1932.summary: In Norton, one of the two medicines, White and Red, which share one vessel and working at first.
E1932.body: Norton (quoted): the White and Red medicines share one vessel and working at first, and seeking further is useless “Till the white medicine be fully wrought.” [IV.2 ¶13].

E1933.summary: In Eudoxus, one of the two Mercuries, identified with the Lunaria and called by others the bath of the Moon.
E1933.body: Eudoxus (quoted): “The Lunaria is the White Mercury”, and “the White Mercury is the bath of the Moon” [IV.3 ¶10].
